newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Hindu nationalist party in trouble.
newsitem.headline: India's Hindu nationalist party in trouble.

text.p: India's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), reeling from electoral setbacks in two key states, faced further problems on Sunday over a revolt by state deputies, party leaders said.
The Indian Express newspaper said on Sunday four BJP ministers in the New Delhi state government were reprimanded by the party for seeking to topple the local chief minister.
BJP leaders accused Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front alliance of seeking to destablise the party by fomenting dissidence within its ranks.

"None of this is possible without the blessings of the people in power," a BJP official said, confirming the report. "As such there are no major difference in the party, only those that are promoted by our rivals."

The news followed a big poll stateback to the party in the most populous state of Uttar Pradesh where the BJP won just 177 seats in the 425-member assembly, belying opinion poll predictions of enough seats to form its own government there.

The BJP also lost seven races for 10 assembly seats in the country's largest state of Madhya Pradesh where by-elections this month returned the Congress Party of former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao.
Both the states were once ruled by the BJP and are regarded as launching pads for the party's quest for federal power.

"There are differences within the party and there is a need for a focused agenda," BJP Vice President K.R. Malkani told Reuters. "Among the more important problems to be tackled is a need for clarity in our economic policy."
Malkani was reflecting on at least two major lobbies within the BJP, one cautiously supporting foreign investments, the other taking a more hardline approach against foreign firms.
But politicians said the BJP's troubles had gone beyond the realms of economic policy differences.
The party was able to form a minority national government in May for two weeks after parliamentary elections returned it with 161 seats in the 545-member lower house.

The BJP's hopes of getting crucial support in parliament at that time hinged on its more widely accepted leader Atal Behari Vajpayee's ability to woo opponents. But he resigned as prime minister after two weeks of failed bargaining.

Vajpayee, a moderate Hindu leader, was also blamed later by hardline supporters of the BJP for the party's embarassment in Uttar Pradesh, saying he did not back their campaign for a Hindu temple in the Uttar Pradesh town of Ayodhya.

On the margins of political power until 1989 when it had just two deputies in parliament, the BJP became India's main opposition party over its campaign to build a temple to Lord Rama at the site of a 16th century mosque in Ayodhya.
The mosque was razed by Hindu zealots in December 1992, triggering a spate of Hindu-Moslem clashes that killed some 3,000 people.
The mosque's destruction prompted Rao to dismiss four BJP-ruled state governments, including Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh. It could not win back power there again.
Deve Gowda's government last month compounded the BJP's woes when it forced out a BJP government in the western state of Gujarat, following a revolt in a party once known for its disciplined cadres.
The Congress Party, holding the balance of power in the Gujarat state assembly, said last week it would support the formation of a non-BJP government led by the dissidents there.
"Our aim is not to join any government with BJP elements," a Congress leader said. "We want to break their backbone."
